title: Design a ticket booking system
problem: Two hundred thousand fans want five thousand seats in the same minute, and two of them tapping E7 together must not both get a ticket.
summary: A booking system caches the seat map, queues the crowd in a virtual waiting room, and lets one database transaction decide each seat: a hold with a TTL taken under row locks, an idempotent confirm, and a payment timeout that releases the seats.
catTip: I nap on the box with the seats, and nobody gets E7 until I say so. The map on the wall can run a second behind and the queue outside can be long, but the box answers once per seat.

recall.q: An IPL final puts 5,000 seats in front of 200,000 fans in one minute. What is the key design decision, and what hangs off it?
recall.a: Queue the people, cache the map, and let the database decide the seat. A waiting room admits fans at the rate holds can be made (free seats divided by seats per hold, with a margin for abandons), the seat map is a cached snapshot that may be a second stale, and each hold is one transaction under SELECT FOR UPDATE NOWAIT with a TTL, an idempotent confirm on the payment id, and a payment timeout that releases the seats.

guide.breaks: Two fans read seat E7 as free in the same millisecond and both are told to pay, or a sale lets 200,000 people hammer the database for 2,000 holds and every show on the platform slows down.
guide.tradeoffs: Holds take seats off the market for ten minutes while carts are abandoned, the seat map is deliberately a second stale, fans wait in a queue even when the site is idle elsewhere, and the write path refuses holds during a database failover rather than risk two owners.
guide.explainSimply: A cloakroom has one attendant and a board of numbered hooks. Everyone in the hall can see the board, a steward lets people in a few at a time, and only the attendant hangs coats, one at a time. If you have not paid for your hook within ten minutes, the coat comes back off.
guide.hint: Separate the three crowds: who looks at the map, who is let in, and who is allowed to write a seat row, then ask which one the database must serve.

meow: Mrrp. Queue the humans, cache the map. One paw on the seat row, one transaction, one ticket. Ten minutes to pay or the seat comes back. Meow.

quiz.prompt: An IPL final releases 5,000 seats at noon and 200,000 fans arrive in the first minute. Where should the design put its first line of defence against the database being overwhelmed?
options: Add PostgreSQL read replicas so seat-map reads stop competing with hold writes
A virtual waiting room that admits fans at roughly the rate holds can be created, with the seat map served from a cache and each admitted hold decided by the database under a row lock
Move seat holds to Redis SET NX with a TTL so the database only sees confirmed bookings
Optimistic locking with a version column so hold attempts never block each other
quiz.explanation: Only the waiting room changes the number of hold attempts the database must refuse, from about 3,300 a second to about 50, and the cache removes the 100k map reads a second. Redis holds are the strongest distractor: they are fast, but a failover loses every hold in flight and a multi-seat hold needs a script, and they still let 3,300 attempts a second through to something.

quiz.prompt: A fan's payment is authorised at 12:10:03 for a hold that expired at 12:10:00, and another fan has already held the same seats. What should the confirm step do?
options: Confirm the paying fan and release the newer hold, because money has changed hands
Lock the hold row, find it released, answer 409 so the payment service cancels the authorisation, and treat this as rare because pay extends the hold before authorising
Automatically book different seats of the same price category for the paying fan
Return 500 so the payment service retries the confirm until the seats free up
quiz.explanation: The hold row in the database is the only decision that counts, and because pay extended the hold before any money moved, a lapsed hold at confirm time is the exception, not the rule. Confirming the payer anyway is the strongest distractor: it would override a hold the database already granted to someone else, which is the double booking the whole design exists to prevent.

cards.q: Problem: two booking servers each read seat E7 as free in the same millisecond during a sold-out drop. Decision and why?
cards.a: Let the database decide inside one transaction: SELECT the requested seats FOR UPDATE NOWAIT in seat-id order, treat a HELD seat whose expiry has passed as free, update them to HELD with a 10-minute expiry and insert the hold, and keep a unique constraint on booked seats as the backstop. NOWAIT fits because the loser wants another seat, not a place in line; a fixed lock order prevents deadlocks; optimistic version checks are cheaper on a quiet day but cause retry storms when 99 attempts in 100 will fail.

cards.q: Problem: 200,000 fans for 2,000 possible holds in the first minute of a sale. Decision and why?
cards.a: A virtual waiting room: an arrival counter gives each fan a number, an admitted counter advances at a pace computed from the inventory (free seats divided by seats per hold, times a margin for abandoned holds, so about 3,000 fans in minute one and then roughly the rate of released and confirmed holds), and an admitted fan gets a signed token the gateway requires on POST /holds. The queue page compares two counters and never touches the database; if the queue store fails, fail open to a per-show rate limit so the sale continues degraded.

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation, SELECT, "The Locking Clause"
sources.supports: FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows against concurrent updates; NOWAIT reports an error rather than waiting if a row cannot be locked immediately; SKIP LOCKED skips rows that cannot be locked and is suggested for multiple consumers on a queue-like table

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation, "Partial Indexes", Example 11.3 Setting up a Partial Unique Index
sources.supports: a unique index with a WHERE predicate enforces uniqueness among the rows that satisfy the predicate only, used here for the insert-only hold variant

sources.title: Redis documentation, SET command
sources.supports: NX sets the key only if it does not exist and EX sets an expiry; SET resource NX EX is described as a simple lock whose release should compare a random token in a script, and the documentation says the pattern is discouraged in favour of Redlock

sources.title: Cloudflare Waiting Room documentation, overview
sources.supports: a virtual waiting room sends excess visitors to a waiting page to protect origin servers from overload, tracks visitors' inflow and outflow, and shows estimated wait times

sources.title: Cloudflare Waiting Room documentation, "Configuration settings"
sources.supports: the total active users cap and the new users per minute threshold, session duration of 1 to 30 minutes with a default of 5, session revocation by the origin through the Cf-Waiting-Room-Command: revoke response header, and a Turnstile challenge mode

sources.title: Stripe API reference, "Idempotent requests"
sources.supports: the Idempotency-Key header; the saved response is returned on a retry; keys may be pruned after 24 hours; a reused key with different parameters is an error; GET and DELETE need no key

sources.title: Stripe documentation, "Place a hold on a payment method"
sources.supports: separate authorisation and capture with capture_method manual; an authorisation for an online card payment is usually valid for 7 days; cancelling before capture releases the held funds, which is what the design does when a hold lapses mid-payment

sources.title: Stripe documentation, "How Payment Intents and Setup Intents work" (lifecycle)
sources.supports: requires_capture after authorisation when capturing separately; cancellation releases any held funds and cannot be undone
